claims.text: A thin, adherent ceramic coating on boride-based components will improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion relative to untreated components.
A thin, dense alumina or TiN coating can be applied by CVD as a uniform, adherent barrier on the component surface.
The ceramic coating will form a continuous physical barrier that minimizes direct contact between molten aluminum and the boride substrate.
Minimizing contact between molten aluminum and the boride substrate will hinder aluminum diffusion and alloy formation.
Reduced interdiffusion and interfacial reaction will prevent rapid formation of deleterious phases and corrosion products.
Suppressing deleterious phases and corrosion products will preserve the integrity of the boride-based component.
Coated samples will exhibit less corrosion penetration than uncoated samples after molten-aluminum exposure.
Coated samples will exhibit lower weight loss than uncoated samples after molten-aluminum exposure.
Coated samples will retain mechanical properties better than uncoated samples after molten-aluminum exposure.
Approximately 660°C represents the typical melting-point temperature of aluminum.
The protective effect should remain effective around 660°C under standard hot-dip aluminum-plating conditions while the coating remains intact.
Mechanical wear, excessive thermal stress, or deposition defects may diminish the coating's protective effect.
Barrier protection is a well-established mechanism.
The magnitude of corrosion improvement is sensitive to coating material, thickness, and deposition quality.
Coated and uncoated samples should be tested under identical molten-aluminum immersion conditions.
Corrosion depth, weight loss, and post-exposure mechanical integrity can be used as response variables.
The hypothesis is falsified if the coating produces no statistically significant reduction in corrosion depth or comparable degradation metrics relative to the uncoated control.
